quiz.title: Chapter 5 Quiz: Case Law
quiz.intro: Ten questions on reading a case for the question you hold, the editorial apparatus, and what a citator actually tracks.

items.q: A case is binding authority only when it comes from:
options: Any court in the United States
A higher court in the same jurisdiction
Any appellate court
A court that published the opinion
items.why: A case from another jurisdiction, a court at the same level, or a lower court is persuasive (The Hierarchy of Case Law Authority).

options: Part of the opinion and citable
An editor-written summary of a point in the case, useful for navigation but carrying no authority
The court’s holding
A citator signal
items.why: Never cite a headnote; only the opinion text carries precedential weight (Headnotes; Common Pitfalls).

items.q: What does a citator such as KeyCite or Shepard’s actually track?
options: The case as a whole
Points of law: later treatment attaches to specific propositions, which is why the analysis is tied to particular headnotes
Only overrulings
Only the cases the opinion cites
items.why: A case overruled on one point can remain solid authority on another; Plessy is the canonical example (Citators).

items.q: A red or yellow citator signal means:
options: The case cannot be cited
The case was reversed on appeal
Read the citing opinions; the signal is a reminder, not a verdict
The case is binding
items.why: Learn the color codes, then read far enough to learn which points of law any negative treatment reaches (Citators).

items.q: Which is the chapter’s test for distinguishing holding from dictum?
options: Whether the statement appears in the majority opinion
Whether the statement was necessary to resolve the dispute before the court
Whether the statement is quoted in a headnote
Whether the statement is more than one sentence
items.why: If the court could have left it out and reached the same result, it is dictum (Holding vs. Dictum).

options: All the facts the court recites
The facts the decision actually turned on, which predict how the rule applies to new facts
The procedural history
The facts in the headnotes
items.why: Dispositive fact identification is the key skill for applying a case to your client’s facts (Case Law and the Research Cycle; Appendix B).

items.q: The five-move protocol for running the cycle through a case begins with:
options: Reading the whole opinion carefully
Bringing the question to the case and keeping the question, not the case, in the foreground
Checking the citator
Reading the dissent
items.why: Then read for the answer, synthesize, log the collateral questions, and choose the next question (Running the Cycle Through a Case).

items.q: Olmstead v. United States is used to illustrate:
options: That wiretapping is always a search
That a dissent can later become the law, so spotting that trajectory early lets you argue for where the law is heading
That concurrences are binding
That the Fourth Amendment protects only property
items.why: Brandeis’s dissent on privacy later became the majority view (Opinions, Concurrences, and Dissents).

items.q: An unpublished opinion you found in a database:
options: Is binding because it is in the database
Can always be cited
May or may not be citable depending on your jurisdiction’s rules, which you must check before citing
Is never persuasive
items.why: Check whether it is published, what your court’s rules say, and what weight it carries (Published vs. Unpublished Opinions).

items.q: The pullquote about the foster mother shows which kind of application question?
options: A fact-finding question squarely answered by a case
A constructive question: the rule’s own exception has to be built from several sources by analogy
A definitional question
A survey question
items.why: Where no decision squarely answers the application, the work is analogical, synthesizing decided applications and arguing which side of the line your facts fall on (Answering Questions with Case Law).
